deep.reconstruction:
There are no derivations on this page. It is a sheet of English-language knot drawings headed 'J.F.E. Gauss. 1794' and 'A collection of knots'. It contains eight numbered pictures of practical ropework.

(1) 'thumb knot, which taylors make use of' is the overhand knot. As a closed curve it would be the trefoil, though no such abstraction appears here.
(2) 'loop knot' is an overhand knot tied in a bight, i.e. an overhand loop.
(3) 'draw knot' is a slipped (quick-release) knot made with a long drawn-through bight.
(4) 'ring knot' is a multiply wrapped knot with three or more parallel turns, possibly a decorative or ring-hitch variant.
(5) is unnamed, a bend or knot with one end hanging down.
(6) 'running knot' is a slip knot or noose, with one strand inked heavily to show its path.
(7) is unnamed, a hitch or mooring knot around a post standing in water, with a half hitch on the standing part.
(8) is unnamed, a bend joining two ropes, with ends labelled a, b (the horizontal parts) and c, d (the crossing ends). The caption reads: 'Drawn at a, b it will close, but drawn at c, d it will open again.' This describes a knot that holds when the standing parts are loaded but capsizes or spills when the ends are pulled. Examples of this behaviour are the reef or square knot, or a slipped bend.

The next page continues the list: 9 fisherman's or water knot, 10 meshing knot, 11 barber's knot, 12 bowline, 13 wale knot. It also has later bibliographic notes (Riedl 1827; 's Gravesande, Philosophiae Newtonianae).

Nothing is computed. The page records physical knot forms, apparently copied from an English source, and documents the young Gauss's early interest in knots. The literature links this interest to his later work on linking numbers (1833) and to the Gauss code (c. 1823–1844).
errors: The caption to (8) is physically plausible: a reef-type or slipped bend closes under tension on the standing parts and spills when the ends are pulled.
Knot (7) is only partly legible as to type. Identifying it as a particular hitch is uncertain.

results.what: Illustrated catalogue of practical knots (overhand, loop, slipped, running knot, hitch on a post, bend), with a remark on knot (8) closing or opening depending on which ends are pulled
results.modern_name: Practical knot catalogue (seamanship knots); overhand knot ~ trefoil
results.usually_credited_to: Traditional seamanship literature; the sheet itself is discussed in histories of knot theory (e.g. M. Epple, Die Entstehung der Knotentheorie, 1999; J. Przytycki's history of knot theory)

deep.surprise_reason: This sheet is well known and has been reproduced and discussed as evidence of Gauss's early (1794) interest in knots. It has no mathematical content beyond drawings copied from a practical source.
transcription_corrections: Top-right shelf mark appears as '487/3' with the '487' struck through, not '48/3'.
